text:
Strong training-pair separation need not imply good top-10 ranking: it measures discrimination against the training sampler, potentially dominated by easy negatives. Krichene and Rendle show sampled Recall/NDCG can reverse full-catalog model ordering even in expectation; with very small samples, metrics approach AUC and lose top-rank sensitivity ([paper](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2021/651)). Relevant 2024 evidence: correcting sampled rank estimates improves WARP/LambdaRank training ([Subbiah et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.06371)); sequential recommendation experiments find random negative sampling favors head items, while popularity-based sampling can improve balance across popularity bands at an overall accuracy cost ([Prakash et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276)). Thus aggregate separation can conceal both candidate-distribution mismatch and popularity-dependent errors.

Diagnostic proposal inferred from these findings: for fixed training-history prefixes and their observed next items, report pairwise outranking probability, counting ties as one-half, against separate uniform, target-popularity-matched, and transition-hard candidate pools. Build popularity bins and transition counts exclusively from training interactions; exclude prefix-seen items and the target from negatives. Also compute full eligible-catalog rank percentile, (rank−1)/(catalog_size−1), with an explicit tie convention; lower is better. These measures are invariant to strictly increasing score transformations, unlike raw logit margins. Report distributions and head/mid/tail breakdowns: excellent uniform discrimination with poor hard-pool ranks suggests unresolved close competitors. Percentile alone can hide consequential top-10 errors in large catalogs, so retain absolute ranks and top-10 membership alongside it. Training-only probes reveal fit and failure patterns, not generalization; unchanged host macro validation HR@10 remains the sole selection metric.
